key_terms.meaning: Current whose magnitude and direction reverse periodically; Indian domestic supply reverses 50 times a second.
v = V<sub>m</sub> sin(ωt + φ), the value of the wave at one particular instant, in volts.
The largest value a sine wave reaches in one cycle, in volts or amperes.
Mean over one half cycle of a sine wave, V<sub>av</sub> = 2V<sub>m</sub>/π = 0.637 V<sub>m</sub>.
Square root of the mean of the squared wave, V<sub>rms</sub> = V<sub>m</sub>/√2 = 0.707 V<sub>m</sub> for a sine.
ω = 2πf rad/s, where f is frequency in hertz.
RMS value ÷ average value; 1.11 for a sine wave, 1.0 for a square wave.
Peak value ÷ RMS value; √2 ≈ 1.414 for a sine wave.
A rotating arrow of length V<sub>rms</sub> (or V<sub>m</sub>) at angle φ used to represent a sinusoid of fixed frequency.
Angle by which one sinusoid leads or lags another of the same frequency, in degrees or radians.
Complex ratio V/I of a circuit, Z = R + jX, measured in ohms (Ω).
Opposition from an inductor, X<sub>L</sub> = 2πfL Ω; current lags voltage by 90° in a pure inductor.
Opposition from a capacitor, X<sub>C</sub> = 1/(2πfC) Ω; current leads voltage by 90° in a pure capacitor.
Y = 1/Z, the ease with which current flows, in siemens (S).
P = VI cos φ, the power that actually does work, in watts (W).
Q = VI sin φ, power that swings between source and L or C, in volt-amperes reactive (VAR).
S = VI = √(P² + Q²), the power equipment must be rated for, in volt-amperes (VA).
cos φ = P/S, a number between 0 and 1; lagging when current lags voltage.
The order in which the three phase voltages reach their positive peaks, e.g. R-Y-B.
Three windings joined at a common neutral point; gives two voltage levels and a fourth wire.
Three windings joined end to end in a closed loop; three wires, no neutral.
Line values are measured between lines; phase values are measured across or through one winding.

takeaways: A coil turning at constant speed in a uniform magnetic field produces e = V<sub>m</sub> sin ωt, so the sine wave is built into every generator.
RMS value is the DC value that would heat a resistor equally; that is why 230 V mains means 230 V RMS and about 325 V peak.
Form factor and peak factor are shape numbers: 1.11 and 1.414 for a sine, 1.0 and 1.0 for a square, and different again for a triangular wave.
A phasor freezes the rotation: length gives magnitude, angle gives phase, and adding phasors by vector rules gives the sum of sinusoids.
In series R-L-C, impedance Z = R + j(X<sub>L</sub> − X<sub>C</sub>) carries both size and phase, so one complex number answers the whole circuit.
Real power P = VI cos φ does work; reactive power Q = VI sin φ only shuttles back and forth; apparent power S = VI sizes the wiring and the transformer.
Star gives √3 times the phase voltage at the lines and a neutral for unbalanced loads; delta gives √3 times the phase current in the lines.
For any balanced three-phase load, total power is √3 V<sub>L</sub> I<sub>L</sub> cos φ, whether the load is in star or in delta.
bank_note: Long answers are expected to combine a labelled phasor or circuit diagram, a clean derivation of the formula, and a numerical check — with star/delta relations and the √3 power formula asked almost every time.

bank.q: Explain how a coil rotating at constant speed in a uniform magnetic field produces a sinusoidal voltage. Write the instantaneous voltage expression and define every symbol in it.
outline: Faraday's law: changing flux linkage induces emf
Flux through coil Φ = BA cos θ with θ = ωt as the coil turns
Result e = NBAω sin ωt, so the waveform is sinusoidal
Define V<sub>m</sub> = NBAω, ω = 2πf, t in seconds
Peak occurs when the coil plane is parallel to the field
One full turn gives one complete cycle; f = N<sub>rpm</sub>/60 for a two-pole machine

bank.q: Define average value and RMS value of a periodic waveform. Derive both for a sine wave and explain why RMS, not average, is used to rate equipment.
outline: Average over half cycle: (1/π)∫V<sub>m</sub> sin θ dθ = 2V<sub>m</sub>/π = 0.637 V<sub>m</sub>
RMS: square, average over full cycle, square root → V<sub>m</sub>/√2 = 0.707 V<sub>m</sub>
Average over a full cycle of a sine is zero, so half-cycle average is used
Heating in a resistor goes as i², so the square-root-of-mean-square is the DC equivalent
230 V mains is RMS; peak is 230√2 ≈ 325 V
Insulation is chosen from peak, heating and rating from RMS

bank.q: Define form factor and peak factor. Compute both for a sinusoidal, a square and a triangular waveform and comment on what the numbers tell you.
outline: Form factor = RMS/average; peak factor = peak/RMS
Sine: 1.11 and 1.414
Square: 1.0 and 1.0 (RMS = peak = average of half cycle)
Triangular: RMS = V<sub>m</sub>/√3, average = V<sub>m</sub>/2, so form factor 1.155 and peak factor √3 ≈ 1.732
A meter calibrated on sine reads wrong on other shapes
Peak factor matters for insulation and for rectifier peak inverse voltage

bank.q: Explain phasor representation of sinusoidal quantities. Why can a sinusoid of fixed frequency be drawn as a stationary arrow, and how are phasors added and subtracted?
outline: A sinusoid has three data: magnitude, frequency, phase
Frequency is the same for all quantities in a linear circuit at steady state, so it can be dropped
Rotating vector of length V<sub>m</sub> at ω, projected on the vertical axis gives v(t)
Freeze the picture at t = 0: length = RMS or peak, angle = phase
Same-frequency phasors add by parallelogram or by resolving into x and y components
Subtraction = add the reversed phasor; results valid only for the same frequency

bank.q: A coil of resistance 8 Ω and inductance 30 mH is connected to a 230 V, 50 Hz supply. Find the impedance, current, phase angle and power factor, and draw the phasor diagram.
outline: φ = tan⁻¹(9.42/8) = 49.7°, current lags
Power factor = cos 49.7° = 0.647 lagging
Phasor diagram: I reference, V<sub>R</sub> in phase, V<sub>L</sub> leading by 90°, supply V the vector sum

bank.q: A series R-L-C circuit has R = 10 Ω, L = 0.1 H, C = 50 µF and is connected to 230 V, 50 Hz. Find Z, I, V<sub>R</sub>, V<sub>L</sub>, V<sub>C</sub> and verify Kirchhoff's voltage law in phasor form.
outline: X<sub>L</sub> = 31.4 Ω, X<sub>C</sub> = 63.7 Ω
X = X<sub>L</sub> − X<sub>C</sub> = −32.3 Ω, so the circuit is capacitive
V<sub>R</sub> = 68 V, V<sub>L</sub> = 214 V, V<sub>C</sub> = 433 V
Phasor sum √(V<sub>R</sub>² + (V<sub>L</sub> − V<sub>C</sub>)²) = 230 V, so KVL holds
Note V<sub>C</sub> exceeds the supply voltage — possible because the voltages are out of phase

bank.q: A 5 kW load runs at 230 V, 50 Hz with a power factor of 0.7 lagging. Find the current and apparent power, then calculate the capacitance needed to raise the power factor to 0.95 lagging.
outline: Reactive power Q<sub>1</sub> = P tan φ<sub>1</sub> = 5 × tan 45.6° = 5.10 kVAR
At 0.95 pf, tan φ<sub>2</sub> = 0.329, Q<sub>2</sub> = 1.64 kVAR
Capacitor must supply Q<sub>C</sub> = 5.10 − 1.64 = 3.46 kVAR
Current falls from 31.1 A to about 22.9 A; cable and transformer loading drop

bank.q: Three identical coils of impedance (6 + j8) Ω per phase are connected in star to a 400 V, 50 Hz three-phase supply. Find phase voltage, phase current, line current and total power.
outline: Star: V<sub>ph</sub> = 400/√3 = 231 V
In star I<sub>L</sub> = I<sub>ph</sub> = 23.1 A
cos φ = R/|Z| = 0.6
P = √3 V<sub>L</sub> I<sub>L</sub> cos φ = √3 × 400 × 23.1 × 0.6 = 9.6 kW
Check: P = 3 I<sub>ph</sub>²R = 3 × 23.1² × 6 = 9.6 kW

bank.q: Draw and explain star and delta connections of three-phase windings. State the voltage and current relations for each and give one practical situation where each is used.
outline: Star: three ends joined at neutral N; line-to-line voltage √3 times phase voltage; I<sub>L</sub> = I<sub>ph</sub>
Phase difference of 30° between line and phase voltage, with a clear phasor diagram
Delta: windings closed in a loop; V<sub>L</sub> = V<sub>ph</sub>; I<sub>L</sub> = √3 I<sub>ph</sub>
Star gives two voltage levels and a neutral — used for distribution and motor starters
Delta used where only one voltage is available and for running motors; a delta-connected winding must never be opened under load

bank.q: Derive the relation between line and phase quantities for a balanced star and a balanced delta load, and hence show that total three-phase power is √3 V<sub>L</sub> I<sub>L</sub> cos φ in both cases.
outline: Balanced phasors 120° apart; vector difference of two phase voltages gives √3 V<sub>ph</sub>
Star: V<sub>L</sub> = √3 V<sub>ph</sub>, I<sub>L</sub> = I<sub>ph</sub>, power = 3 V<sub>ph</sub> I<sub>ph</sub> cos φ
Delta: V<sub>L</sub> = V<sub>ph</sub>, I<sub>L</sub> = √3 I<sub>ph</sub>, power = 3 V<sub>ph</sub> I<sub>ph</sub> cos φ
Substitute in each case and both reduce to √3 V<sub>L</sub> I<sub>L</sub> cos φ
Conclusion: a wattmeter sees the same power whatever the internal connection
Neutral current in a balanced star load is zero, so the neutral can be omitted

bank.q: Compare single-phase and three-phase supply for delivering the same power at the same line voltage. Discuss line current, copper required, torque smoothness and why industry prefers three-phase.
outline: For the same P and V, a single-phase line carries P/(V cos φ); three-phase lines carry P/(√3 V<sub>L</sub> cos φ) each
Three-phase current per conductor is 1/√3 of the single-phase value, so thinner conductors
Total copper for the same loss falls roughly by half; two conductors saved where neutral is not needed
Instantaneous three-phase power is constant, giving steady torque in motors
Three-phase motors are self-starting; single-phase motors need auxiliary windings
Domestic supply still uses single phase because loads are small

bank.q: A series R-L-C circuit is brought to resonance. Explain what happens to impedance, current, the voltages across L and C, and the power factor. Why can V<sub>L</sub> be several times the supply voltage?
outline: At resonance X<sub>L</sub> = X<sub>C</sub>, so X = 0 and Z = R (minimum)
Current is maximum, I = V/R, and in phase with supply; power factor unity
V<sub>L</sub> and V<sub>C</sub> are individually Q times the supply voltage, where Q = X<sub>L</sub>/R
They are 180° apart, so their phasor sum cancels; KVL is still satisfied
Resonant frequency f<sub>r</sub> = 1/(2π√(LC))
Danger: insulation and capacitor ratings must allow for the Q-times voltage; this is how a radio tunes

bank.q: A factory draws 100 kW at a power factor of 0.6 lagging from the supply authority. Explain why the authority penalises this, and evaluate adding a capacitor bank against replacing the motors with high-efficiency ones.
outline: Load current is P/(V cos φ); low pf means larger current for the same kW
Larger current causes higher I²R losses, bigger cables, transformer and switchgear rated in kVA
Apparent power here is 167 kVA for only 100 kW of useful work
Capacitor bank: cheap, static, no moving parts, reduces Q directly; needs switching as load varies and can cause over-correction
Motor replacement: costs more, improves efficiency as well, but does not fix reactive demand unless pf is also improved
Recommend measurement of load profile before choosing; a mixed solution is usually best
Give a sample calculation showing current and kVA before and after correction

glossary.def: The graph of a quantity against time.
One complete set of positive and negative values of a periodic wave.
Time taken for one complete cycle, in seconds; T = 1/f.
Number of cycles per second, in hertz (Hz).
A waveform of the form V<sub>m</sub> sin(ωt + φ), produced by a coil rotating in a uniform magnetic field.
The angle ωt + φ that fixes where the wave is in its cycle at time t.
A current leads when its peak comes earlier than the voltage's, and lags when it comes later.
The part of impedance that stores and returns energy, X = X<sub>L</sub> − X<sub>C</sub>, in ohms.
The part of impedance that converts electrical energy into heat, in ohms.
Z = R + jX, where j = √(−1); both magnitude and phase in one number.
The real part of admittance, G = R/(R² + X²), in siemens.
The imaginary part of admittance, B = −X/(R² + X²), in siemens.
The condition X<sub>L</sub> = X<sub>C</sub> at which impedance is purely resistive and current is maximum.
p = vi at one instant; for a sine supply it swings at twice the supply frequency.
The unit of apparent power, written VA; kVA is 1000 VA.
A three-phase load whose three phase impedances are identical in magnitude and angle.
The fourth wire in a star system, joined to the common point of the three windings.
Voltage across one phase winding, measured between a line and the neutral in star.
Voltage between any two line conductors.
Current flowing through one phase winding of the load.
Current flowing in a line conductor supplying the load.
Three voltages of equal magnitude, 120° apart, from one generator.
